title.text: Finding structure without labels: customer segments and unusual orders

objects.text: How do we group customers, or spot odd cases, when nobody gave us the answers?

AI and Data Science Professional  |  Session 18 of 24  |  Module D: Machine learning
KLAi Professional Learning  |  Jotham Martin Wambi

slides.notes:
Welcome back. Last session we learned to get a stronger model without fooling ourselves, and we saw that the simple model often wins. Today there is no answer column at all. We take the Lakeside Mart orders and ask who our customers are, in groups a manager can describe.

We prepare three numbers per customer, let k-means find the groups, name them, and flag unusual orders. The test is whether you could take the result into a meeting.

slides.notes:
Here is what you can do by the end of today. You can build recency, frequency and monetary value for each customer, and prepare them with a log transform and standardisation. You can run k-means clustering, choose the number of groups with the elbow method, squeeze three variables into two with principal component analysis, and give each segment a name a manager can use.

And you can flag unusual orders and customers with a percentile rule and an isolation forest, and say what to do with them. We use the Lakeside Mart orders for all of it. There is no answer column today.

title.text: Your two hours: concepts first, then a Python lab

objects.text: Ideas with pictures first. Then you open the notebook. Then the checks and what you keep.

slides.notes:
We have two hours. The first ten minutes bring back Session 17 and set the question for today. Then forty-five minutes of concepts, with no laptops open, so you can watch the pictures and the worked numbers. After a ten minute break we open the notebook for a forty-five minute lab on the Lakeside Mart customers.

You will predict each result, run it, read it, and change one thing. The last ten minutes are an exit check and what you keep. The lab is where the learning sticks, so please protect that time.

title.text: Three questions from last time

runs.text: 1.  A model scores very well on its training rows and much worse on its test rows. What is that called?
2.  A forest reports a high permutation importance for one variable. What can you safely say?
3.  Two models score about the same. Which one do you ship, and what is the rule called?

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_question_2.80.png

objects.text: Answer aloud first. Then we check together.

slides.notes:
Three quick questions from Session 17. Answer aloud first, and then we check together. It is a warm-up to bring last time back.

Question one. A model scores very well on its training rows and much worse on its test rows. What is that called?

A good answer is this. Overfitting. The distance between the two scores is the generalisation gap.

Question two. A forest reports a high permutation importance for one variable. What can you safely say?

A good answer is this. The model relies on that variable. It does not show a cause.

Question three. Two models score about the same. Which one do you ship, and what is the rule called?

A good answer is this. The simpler one. The rule is parsimony.

If you missed one, check your notes from last session tonight. Now to today.

title.text: Answers to the three questions from Session 17

rows.text: A model scores very well on its training rows and much worse on its test rows. What is that called?
Overfitting. The distance between the two scores is the generalisation gap.
A forest reports a high permutation importance for one variable. What can you safely say?
The model relies on that variable. It does not show a cause.
Two models score about the same. Which one do you ship, and what is the rule called?
The simpler one. The rule is parsimony.

Here are the answers to the three warm-up questions. A model that scores very well on its training rows and much worse on its test rows is overfitting, and the distance between the two scores is the generalisation gap. A high permutation importance tells you the model relies on that variable.

It does not show that the variable causes the outcome. And when two models score about the same, you ship the simpler one, which is the rule of parsimony. Today we leave answer columns behind. Which of the three did you find hardest?

title.text: Words we use today

rows.text: Unsupervised learning (for example clustering, anomaly detection)
Learning with no answer column. The algorithm looks for groups or odd rows by itself.
Three numbers per customer: recency (days since the last order), frequency (number of orders) and monetary value (total spend).
Standardisation (z-score) puts variables on one scale. A log transform squeezes a long right tail.
Splits records into k clusters around k centroids. Inertia measures how tight they are. The elbow method suggests k.
A dimensionality reduction method: it mixes many variables into a few principal components that keep most of the variance.

slides.notes:
Five words for today. I give the plain meaning of each, and we use every one of them before the end of the session.

Unsupervised learning (for example clustering, anomaly detection). Learning with no answer column. The algorithm looks for groups or odd rows by itself.

RFM analysis. Three numbers per customer: recency (days since the last order), frequency (number of orders) and monetary value (total spend).

Feature scaling and log transform. Standardisation (z-score) puts variables on one scale. A log transform squeezes a long right tail.

k-means clustering. Splits records into k clusters around k centroids. Inertia measures how tight they are. The elbow method suggests k.

Principal component analysis (PCA). A dimensionality reduction method: it mixes many variables into a few principal components that keep most of the variance.

title.text:
Supervised learning has an answer
column. Unsupervised learning has none

objects.text: Sessions 14 to 17: supervised

runs.text: The loans table has a default column.
The model learns to predict it.
We score it against the known answer.

objects.text: Today: unsupervised

runs.text: The orders have no segment column.
We look for structure, then judge it ourselves.

objects.text: No accuracy to chase. Inertia and the silhouette score help. A person judges.

slides.notes:
Everything so far had an answer column. In the loan data each loan said whether it defaulted, so the model could learn from it and we could score it afterwards. That is supervised learning. Today the orders have no segment column. Nobody went through the customers and wrote down who is a big spender or who has drifted away.

The algorithm must look for structure by itself. That is unsupervised learning, and grouping records is called clustering. The consequence matters. With no known answer there is no AUC to chase, so a person has to decide whether the groups make sense for the business. Internal measures such as inertia and the silhouette score help you compare choices of k.

Also remember that k-means assumes round clusters of similar size. Where would you want groups of customers at your work?

title.text:
Walk-in orders have no customer_id, so 30
percent of orders cannot join a customer segment

objects.text: 9,171 of 30,229 orders are walk-ins. We keep the 21,058 loyalty orders, from 2,499 customers.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_waffle_4.40x4.30_9c5f0f62.png
objects.alt: Walk-in orders have no customer_id, so 30 percent of orders cannot join a customer segment

slides.notes:
Our file is the Lakeside Mart orders again, 30,229 orders from 2024-01-01 to 2025-12-28. To group customers, every order we use must say which customer it belongs to. A walk-in order has a blank customer id, so we cannot follow that person across visits. That is 9,171 orders, about 30 in every hundred, and they are left out of the segments.

Anyone reading your segments must know that walk-in shoppers are not in them. What remains is 21,058 loyalty orders from 2,499 customers. The customers file lists 2,500, so 1 loyalty customer never ordered. Why is it honest to say that out loud?

title.text:
RFM analysis turns one customer's orders into three
numbers: recency, frequency and monetary value

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_i_rfm_11.90x4.25_901d681d.png
objects.alt: RFM analysis turns one customer's orders into three numbers: recency, frequency and monetary value

objects.text: One record per customer: C0001 made 15 orders, the last on 2025-12-22.

slides.notes:
Most customer segments start from three numbers, and the set has a name: RFM analysis. R is recency, the days from the customer's last order to the last date in the file. F is frequency, the number of orders. M is monetary value, the total spent. Take customer C0001.

The picture shows the last five of 15 orders. The last was on 2025-12-22, which is 6 days before the end of the file on 2025-12-28. The customer made 15 orders and spent 969,690 shillings in total. We use the last date in the file as today, so the numbers stay the same each time you open the notebook.

In Excel this is a pivot table with the customer on the rows. Which of the three would a shop manager care about most?

objects.text: Each record is one loyalty customer. The mean spend is above the median: a few large spenders pull it up.

slides.notes:
Here is the result in pandas. Each record is one loyalty customer, so there are 2,499 records and three variables. The first three customers are shown, then the mean, the median and the standard deviation of each variable. Look at monetary value. The mean is 399,687 shillings but the median is 290,090.

When the mean sits well above the median, a few big spenders are pulling it up. That is a right-skewed variable, with a long right tail. Recency is the same: mean 78.5 days, median 46. The three variables are also on very different scales, from a few orders to hundreds of thousands of shillings.

Both facts matter for k-means. What do you notice about the standard deviations?

title.text:
A log transform squeezes the long right tail:
the skewness of spend falls from 3.09 to -0.01

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_i_hist2_11.90x4.25_5daa4240.png
objects.alt: A log transform squeezes the long right tail: the skewness of spend falls from 3.09 to -0.01

objects.text: Skewness measures lopsidedness. We log all three variables: frequency goes from 0.37 to -0.65.

slides.notes:
Spend has a long right tail, so a few customers sit far from the rest. The skewness of spend is 3.09. Skewness measures how lopsided a variable is, and zero means symmetric. A log transform replaces each value by its logarithm. It squeezes big values a lot and small values a little, like a log scale on an Excel chart.

After the transform the skewness of spend is -0.01, so the histogram is roughly symmetric. We use log of one plus x, called log1p, so a value of zero would not break the logarithm. Recency also has a right tail, and its skewness falls from 2.19 to -0.53.

Frequency was only mildly skewed (0.37) and becomes slightly left-skewed (-0.65). Many analysts log only spend. We log all three for one simple recipe. Why would k-means treat a skewed variable badly?

title.text:
Standardisation turns each variable into a z-score:
how many standard deviations from the mean

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_math_11.90x2.33_afd9bd70.png
objects.alt: Standardisation turns each variable into a z-score: how many standard deviations from the mean

rows.text: The value of one customer: here the log of spend
The mean and the standard deviation of that variable over all customers
The z-score: 0 is average, +1 is one standard deviation above

objects.text: Computed from unrounded values, so a hand calculation differs by 0.01. In scikit-learn: StandardScaler.

slides.notes:
Standardisation, also called the z-score, rewrites each variable so its mean is zero and its standard deviation is one. Subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation. Take customer C0001. The log of spend is 13.78. The mean of log spend is 12.61 and the standard deviation is 0.75.

So the z-score is 1.57. That customer is one and a half standard deviations above the average spender. Zero means average, and minus one means one standard deviation below. In scikit-learn the tool is StandardScaler. Why is a z-score easier to compare across variables than the raw value?

title.text:
Feature scaling puts recency, frequency and spend
on one scale before k-means measures distance

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_clock_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_receipt_0.39.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_coin_0.39.png

objects.text: k-means uses distance. Without scaling, spend (in shillings) would decide almost every distance and the other two would count for nothing.

slides.notes:
Why scale at all?

k-means works with distance between customers. The raw standard deviation of recency is 88.7 days, of frequency 2.9 orders, and of spend 374,078 shillings. If we feed those to k-means, spend decides almost every distance, because its numbers are thousands of times bigger. Recency and frequency would count for nothing.

After the log transform and standardisation, every variable has a standard deviation of one, so each gets an equal say. This is called feature scaling. Distance-based methods such as k-means and k-nearest neighbours need it. Which other method from this course used distance?

title.text:
k-means clustering repeats two
moves until the groups stop changing

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_flow_11.90x3.90_163a6732.png
objects.alt: k-means clustering repeats two moves until the groups stop changing

objects.text: k is the number of clusters you choose. A centroid is the mean point of a cluster. Inertia is the sum of squared distances from each customer to its centroid.

slides.notes:
Here is k-means in four moves. You choose k, the number of clusters, and the algorithm starts with k centre points. Move one, assign: put each customer in the cluster with the nearest centre, which is called a centroid. Move two, update: move each centroid to the mean of the customers now in its cluster.

Move three, repeat: assign again with the new centroids. Move four, converge: stop when no customer changes cluster. The number we track is inertia, the sum of squared distances from each customer to its centroid. It can only fall or stay the same at each step. The following picture shows these moves on ten real customers.

Why must the loop end?

title.text:
k-means on ten real customers: the centroids
move and the inertia falls until nothing changes

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_i_moves_11.90x4.25_383d1d83.png
objects.alt: k-means on ten real customers: the centroids move and the inertia falls until nothing changes

objects.text: k = 2. Inertia falls from 17.41 to 7.51 in 3 updates.

slides.notes:
Here are the four moves on ten real customers, with two variables and k equal to two. The gold squares are the centroids, and the filled and hollow dots are the two clusters. On the left we start with two centroids and assign each customer to the nearest one.

The inertia is 17.41. Then each centroid moves to the mean of its cluster, and we assign again. The inertia falls to 9.04, then 7.82. On the right, after 3 updates, no customer changes cluster, so the algorithm has converged at 7.51. Our real run uses all 2,499 customers and three variables, and the same two moves.

Where did the centroids move to?

title.text:
The elbow method plots inertia
against k and looks for the bend

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_i_curves_7.70x4.80_9bf11b5a.png
objects.alt: The elbow method plots inertia against k and looks for the bend

objects.text: Inertia always falls as k grows. Look for where the fall slows.

runs.text: The bend is gentle, so 3, 4 or 5 are all defensible.
We pick 4: four segments can each be named and acted on.

slides.notes:
How do we choose k?

The elbow method plots inertia against k. With k equal to one, the inertia is 7,497, which is three variables times 2,499 customers. It falls as k grows, always. We look for the bend, where extra groups buy little. Here it falls by 2,642 from one to two, 1,023 from two to three, about 700 from three to four, and about 365 from four to five.

The bend is gentle. The elbow is a hint, and the final choice is a judgement. We choose four, because we can name four segments and give each a different action. That is a business reason, and we say so. Would you choose three?

title.text:
Four customer segments on recency and
spend: the groups touch, so the edges are soft

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_i_segments_11.90x4.25_f14ff868.png
objects.alt: Four customer segments on recency and spend: the groups touch, so the edges are soft

objects.text: One dot per customer (2,499). Colours are k-means segments; your run differs by up to 5 percent.

slides.notes:
Here are all the customers on two of the three variables, recency across and spend up, both on log scales. The colours are the four segments k-means found using all three variables. Notice that the clouds touch. There is no gap that separates the groups, because customers behave on a continuum.

The segments are slices of that cloud, and the edges are soft. That is normal for customer data, and it is why we treat segments as useful groupings and never as natural facts. The names on the right come from the next two slides. Where would you draw the line between the red and the black dots?

title.text:
What each segment is like: how far its
average sits from the average customer

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_i_centroids_11.90x4.25_2920d35f.png
objects.alt: What each segment is like: how far its average sits from the average customer

objects.text: Bars: standard deviations from the average customer. Red above, black below.

slides.notes:
To name a segment, read its average against the average customer, in standard deviations. Remember that high recency is bad: it means a long time since the last order. The first segment sits high on frequency and spend and low on recency: frequent, recent, big spenders. We call them best customers.

The second has high recency, so it has been away a while, with about average frequency and spend: drifting regulars. The third has very low recency, so it ordered recently, with about average spend: recent regulars. The fourth is high on recency and low on frequency and spend: lapsed low spenders.

The names are our judgement, and a colleague might choose others. Do these names fit what you would expect?

Naming each segment in business
words: who they are, in real units

objects.text: Averages per customer; your own run differs by up to about 5 percent. Share of spend is out of 998,818,340 UGX.

slides.notes:
Here are the segments in real units, as averages per customer. The best customers are 23 percent of customers and 48 percent of all spend: 833,080 shillings each, 11.5 orders, last seen 40 days ago. The drifting regulars are the biggest group, 898 customers, with 30 percent of spend, but they last ordered 112 days ago.

The recent regulars ordered 11 days ago on average. The lapsed low spenders have only 4.7 orders and 7 percent of spend. A table like this is what you take into a meeting. Which row would you worry about first?

title.text:
A segment is only useful if each
name comes with an action

rows.text: 576 customers; last order 40 days ago; 11.5 orders
Protect them: early access to promotions and one named contact.
898 customers; last order 112 days ago; 8.5 orders
Win them back before they lapse: a reminder offer in the next month.
560 customers; last order 11 days ago; 8.3 orders
Grow the basket: promote higher-value products to them.
465 customers; last order 143 days ago; 4.7 orders
Send a low-cost reactivation message and do not spend heavily.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_coin_0.50.png
/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_clock_0.50.png

/sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_person_0.50.png

slides.notes:
A segment is only useful if the name leads to an action. For the best customers we protect them with early access and a named contact. For the drifting regulars, who are the largest group and are slipping away, a reminder offer in the next month. For the recent regulars we try to grow the basket with higher-value products.

And for the lapsed low spenders we send a low-cost message and do not spend heavily. These actions are our proposals. The test of a segmentation is whether the manager can act on it on Monday. Which action would cost the least to try?

slides.notes:
k-means starts from random centroids, so different starts can end in slightly different answers. We ran it sixty times. The inertia stays between 3,129 and 3,130, so all the answers are about equally good. But the segment sizes move: the largest segment is between 870 and 902 customers, and the third segment varies by 67.

That is what we expect when the clouds touch. Fix the random state so your result is reproducible, and do not quote a segment size to the last customer. Always say these are useful groupings, with soft edges. How would you tell a manager that?

title.text:
PCA squeezes three variables into two principal
components that keep about 86 percent of the variance

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_i_pca_11.90x4.25_d88f446d.png
objects.alt: PCA squeezes three variables into two principal components that keep about 86 percent of the variance

objects.text: Dimensionality reduction: fewer variables, same customers. Colours are the k-means segments.

slides.notes:
Three variables cannot be drawn on a flat page, so we use principal component analysis, or PCA. It is a dimensionality reduction method. It builds new variables, called principal components, each a weighted mix of the originals. The first component is the direction in which the customers vary most.

It carries 57 percent of the variance. The second carries 29 percent, and the third 14. The first two together keep 86 percent, so a flat picture loses little. The colours are the segments from k-means. They overlap in the middle, because the clouds touch and the segments are slices of one cloud.

The picture is for drawing and checking. We use PCA to draw and to check, and k-means ran on all three variables. What does explained variance tell you?

title.text:
Each principal component is a weighted
mix of recency, frequency and spend

objects.text: The sign of a component is arbitrary: flipping every sign gives the same picture. Components are listed from most to least variance.

slides.notes:
This table shows the recipe for each principal component. The first component gives frequency and spend large weights of the same sign, -0.66 and -0.63, and recency the opposite sign, +0.41. So it reads as overall engagement: frequent, big-spending, recent customers at one end and the reverse at the other.

The second component is mostly recency, with a weight of -0.90. The last row shows the explained variance. The sign of a component is arbitrary, so your notebook may show the picture flipped. The components are ordered by how much variance they carry. Which original variable does the second component follow?

title.text:
Anomaly detection, rule one: flag orders
above the 99th percentile (the percentile rule)

objects.text: 303 of 30,229 orders are above the 99th percentile, 468,620 UGX. Median of flagged: 829,200 UGX. Median of all orders: 23,200 UGX.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_waffle_4.40x4.30_daa51afb.png
objects.alt: Anomaly detection, rule one: flag orders above the 99th percentile (the percentile rule)

slides.notes:
The second half of today is anomaly detection: finding records that look very different from the rest, also called outlier detection. The simplest tool is the percentile rule. Sort all the orders by value and flag those above the 99th percentile, which is 468,620 shillings. That flags 303 of 30,229 orders, about one in a hundred.

The median of the flagged orders is 829,200 shillings, against 23,200 for all orders. 90 of the flagged orders are walk-ins. The rule is simple and transparent, and it always flags exactly one percent whether or not anything is wrong. It also looks at one variable at a time.

What might it miss?

title.text:
An isolation forest isolates an odd record with
few random cuts, and a typical record needs many

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/x_ds_i_isodemo_11.90x4.25_5e7927f2.png
objects.alt: An isolation forest isolates an odd record with few random cuts, and a typical record needs many

objects.text: Mean of 300 runs: 2.7 and 9.8 cuts. The real forest uses 100 trees on 256 customers each.

slides.notes:
IsolationForest works on a different idea. Cut the data with random lines, each one across a random variable at a random value, until a record sits alone. An odd record, far from the cloud, is isolated after very few cuts. A typical record, deep inside the cloud, needs many.

In this run the odd customer is alone after 2 cuts and the typical one needs 10. Averaged over 300 runs, it is 2.7 cuts and 9.8. The forest repeats this with many random trees and turns the average number of cuts into an anomaly score. A short path means a high score.

The picture uses forty customers and two variables to keep it readable. Why does this idea need no answer column?

slides.notes:
We ran an isolation forest on the 2,499 customers, using the three scaled variables, and flagged the most isolated one percent, which is 25 customers. The top three are shown, with the median of all the flagged and of all customers. Of the 25 flagged, 12 are customers who have been away a long time and spent little, 7 spent more than eight hundred thousand shillings, and 6 are mixed.

This is our own NumPy version of the algorithm. Run with a different random seed, it flags a list that overlaps ours on 22 of 25, and scikit-learn will differ a little too. Anomaly detection is a way to choose what to look at. Which of these would you check first?

title.text:
An anomaly is a record to review, and
the review decides what happens

objects.text: Flagging is the start of the work.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_magnifier_0.70.png

objects.text: Check for an error: a typing slip, a duplicate or a test order.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_people_0.70.png

objects.text: Check for a real and important case: a wholesale buyer or a fraud.

objects.path: /sessions/focused-youthful-einstein/mnt/IUEA-Teaching-Resources/Professional_AI_Training/Business_AI/AI and Data Science Professional/05 Course Maintenance/KLAi Build/figures/icon_doc_0.70.png

objects.text: Record the decision and the reason.

slides.notes:
What do you do with a flagged record?

You review it. First check for an error: a typing slip, a duplicate or a test order. If it is an error, correct it or exclude it, and write down why. Second, check whether it is real and important. A very large order might be a wholesale buyer you want to look after, or a fraud you want to stop.

A customer who stopped ordering might be about to leave for a competitor. Third, record your decision and the reason. Never delete an anomaly just because an algorithm flagged it. Who would review flagged records in your organisation?

title.text:
Read the recipe before the
lab: log, scale, cluster, profile

objects.text: In plain words

runs.text: Line 1 takes the log of each variable, then scales it to a z-score.
Line 2 sets k = 4, 10 random starts, and fixes the random state.
Line 3 fits k-means and stores each customer's segment number.
Line 5 profiles each segment in real units.

slides.notes:
Before the lab, read the recipe. Line one takes the log of each of the three RFM variables with log one p, then scales them with StandardScaler. Line two creates the KMeans model with four clusters, ten random starts, and a fixed random state so you can repeat it.

Line three fits it and stores each customer's segment number as a new column. Line four prints the inertia, the number we use for the elbow. Line five groups by segment and takes the mean of each variable, which is the profile we name. The segment numbers zero to three are only labels, and they can change from run to run.

Why do the labels have no meaning on their own?

title.text: Five likely mistakes in the lab and how to fix them

rows.text: The walk-in orders (blank customer_id) are still in.
Drop the blank customer_id values first, with dropna on customer_id.
The end date came from today's date.
Use the last order_date in the file as the end date.
Segment 0 is different from the slide
The segment numbers are only labels.
Apply log1p and StandardScaler before KMeans.
The data were not standardised, or a row was dropped.
Three standardised variables over 2,499 customers give 7,497.

slides.notes:
Five situations you may meet. If you get more customers than expected, the walk-in orders are still in, so drop the blank customer ids first. If recency looks wrong, you used today's date, so use the last order date in the file instead. If your segment zero looks different from the slide, that is fine, because the numbers are only labels, so match the segments by their averages.

If spend dominates, you forgot to scale. And the inertia for k equal to one should be seven thousand four hundred and ninety seven: three standardised variables times the number of customers. Which of these would you have guessed?

title.text:
Exit check: three questions, then
compare with the short answers

rows.text: Why do we take the log of spend and then standardise before k-means?
The log squeezes the long tail (skewness 3.09 to -0.01). Standardising gives the three variables one scale, so none dominates the distance.
The elbow chart bends gently between k = 3 and k = 5. How do you choose k?
Treat the elbow as a hint. Choose the k whose segments you can name and act on, and say it is a judgement.
An isolation forest flags 25 customers. What do you do next?
Review each one: an error, or a real and important case. Record the decision. Never delete them automatically.
